title: Standards adapter contract
description: How one standards pack declares the way it is invoked and the way its result is read. The pack owns its contract; StandardsEnforcer owns this schema. Declarative only — no code, no command semantics, no discovery. Every field below was forced by a real pack recorded in artifacts/evidence/2026-08-09-interface-inventory.md; a field nothing forced is absent, and adding one is a schemaVersion change.

schemaVersion.description: Matched exactly against the set this enforcer implements. An unrecognised version is ENFORCEMENT_ERROR, never a best-effort read — the enforcer must not guess what a contract it does not understand is asking for. The version is not a label: it selects which placeholders may appear in `evaluation.arguments`. 1.0.0 admits {target} alone; 1.1.0 additionally admits {policy}. A 1.0.0 contract using {policy} is a violation and not an implicit upgrade, because widening what 1.0.0 admits would retroactively change the meaning of every contract already released under it — and a pack cannot re-release history. A 1.1.0 contract is correctly unreadable to an enforcer built before 1.1.0 existed: that enforcer rejects it on this field rather than dropping the binding it cannot perform.

id.description: Stable identifier for the pack, used to name it in the enforcer's result. Not a display name and never reused.

entrypoint.description: Path to the CLI within the pack's own checkout. FORCED BY PredictionStandards, whose entry is scripts/predictions.mjs where every other pack uses scripts/standards.mjs.

arguments.description: The authoritative verdict invocation, literally. FORCED BY the divergence in every dimension at once: the verdict subcommand is `validate` in Engineering, Betting, Mathematics and Innovation, `check` in Financial and Health, and `evaluate` in MachineLearning; the target is positional in some and `--dir=<path>` in others; and Financial takes `--policy <path>` space-separated where others use `=`. No aliasing, preference ordering or discovery may be inferred from this array — `check` exists in Betting and Innovation and answers a DIFFERENT question in both, executing cleanly and returning a verdict-shaped object, so a pack that does not name its verdict command literally cannot be invoked safely. The {policy} placeholder, admitted from schemaVersion 1.1.0, is FORCED BY FinancialStandards: its `check` resolves an absent `--policy` to the standards pack's OWN project-policy.yml, so pointed at a target it audits the target's documents against Financial's policy, labels the report `"project": "FinancialStandards"`, and exits 0 — a confident verdict about the wrong thing, recorded as finding F of artifacts/evidence/2026-08-09-interface-inventory.md. {target} cannot express it: {target} names the subject being evaluated, {policy} names the governing policy, and a contract that conflated them would evaluate the subject against itself. Financial's form is `--policy <path>` as two argv elements; a contract declaring `--policy={policy}` would be rejected by Financial's own parser as an unknown flag, so the array is the exact argv and the enforcer never joins, splits or reorders it.

contains.description: At least one argument must carry the {target} placeholder, so a contract cannot declare an invocation that never says what to evaluate. Matched as a SUBSTRING, not as a whole argument: Betting passes the target positionally as `{target}` while MachineLearning, Mathematics and Innovation embed it as `--dir={target}`. This was written as `const` until 2026-08-10, which admitted only the positional form — a constraint that excluded three of the four released contracts and went unnoticed for as long as nothing executed the schema. See artifacts/evidence/2026-08-10-conformance-boundary-built.md.

statuses.description: The pack's COMPLETE status vocabulary, read from the top-level `status` key of its JSON. Required so that an unrecognised status fails closed rather than being treated as merely not-passing: those are different problems. FORCED BY the vocabularies not being one alphabet — Engineering has four values and no BLOCKED_BY_INVARIANT, and PredictionStandards uses SUPPORTED / SUPPORTED_WITH_EXCEPTIONS / INSUFFICIENTLY_SUPPORTED.

passing.description: The closed subset of `statuses` on which a merge may proceed, declared by the pack. Present not because the packs disagree — all six provable packs pass on COMPLIANT and COMPLIANT_WITH_EXCEPTIONS — but because ADR 0001 forbids the enforcer holding the knowledge that COMPLIANT means passing. A status outside this set is not passing, including one outside `statuses` entirely.

$absentByDesign.statusPath: Every provable pack puts its verdict at the top-level `status` key, so nothing forced a path expression. PredictionStandards would have — and its integration is blocked for a different reason: it publishes no authoritative status at all.
$absentByDesign.exitCodes: Nothing forced it, and interpreting exit codes would mislead. Betting exits 2 on NOT_EVALUATED with valid JSON, MachineLearning exits 3 on blocked, Health exits 4 on NOT_EVALUATED, and Financial collapses blocked into 1. Parseable JSON carrying a declared status is the signal that the pack ran; the exit code is process semantics and the enforcer does not read it as a verdict.
$absentByDesign.runtime: All eight are Node. Nothing forced the field; the first non-Node pack forces it and a schemaVersion bump.
$absentByDesign.workingDirectory: Tested rather than assumed. No pack requires its own checkout as cwd — Financial ignores cwd entirely, Engineering and MachineLearning default to it and are given {target} explicitly regardless.
$absentByDesign.output: All eight write JSON to stdout under --json. Nothing forced a declaration.
$absentByDesign.versionSource: All eight carry a VERSION file and the enforcer reads it. Note that package.json disagrees with VERSION in Engineering, Financial and Innovation, so the choice matters — but no pack forces it to be declarative.
